original_interpretation: In its Spring 2026 forecast WSTS expected 2026 growth of 20% for microprocessors, 10% for analog, 8% for discretes and 3% for sensors and optoelectronics.
evidence_found: "Other product categories are forecast to expand at more moderate rates, reflecting a broader industry growth: Microprocessors 20 percent, Analog 10 percent, Discrete Semiconductors 8 percent, Sensors and Optoelectronics with 3 percent." (WSTS release, 2 June 2026, p. 1); table 2026: Micro 19.8, Analog 10.2, Discretes 8.0, Optoelectronics 2.7, Sensors 3.0
notes: Correctly framed as the Spring forecast. 'Microprocessors' in the release is the WSTS Micro line (MPU+MCU+DSP); opto is 2.7%, rounded to 3%. Newer: the August 2026 WSTS Q2 update recalculates 2026 at roughly micro 25%, analog 11%, discretes 12%, opto 8%, sensors 2% (chart image). This is recorded as a new claim; it does not make the claim as worded wrong.

original_interpretation: WSTS final 2025 data show discretes at US$30.7bn (-1.0%) while every other product category grew, with sensors +10.4% and optoelectronics +4.7%.
evidence_found: Spring 2026 table, 2025 column (US$M, YoY %): "Discrete Semiconductors 30,728 ... -1.0"; "Optoelectronics 43,042 ... 4.7"; "Sensors 20,894 ... 10.4"; "Analog 86,519 ... 8.7"; "Micro 84,867 ... 7.9"; "Logic 299,547 ... 38.8"; "Memory 230,042 ... 39.0" (WSTS, 2 June 2026, p. 2)
notes: The table does not label 2025 as 'final'. It is the full-year 2025 actual inside a June 2026 forecast release, so 'final' means WSTS's published full-year actual. The Q2 2026 chart (SRC-0245) also shows 2025 Discretes at -1%.

original_interpretation: WSTS attributed the expected slight 2025 decline in discretes mainly to ongoing weakness in automotive applications.
evidence_found: "The Discretes product segment is expected to decline slightly, mainly due to ongoing weakness in automotive applications." (WSTS Autumn 2025 release, 2 Dec 2025, p. 1); table: Discrete Semiconductors 2025 -0.4%
notes: This is WSTS's own explanation, so reported_claim is the right type. The outcome held: the full-year 2025 actual was -1.0% (SRC-0001).

original_interpretation: In the WSTS classification, Total Logic (L99) is made up of digital bipolar (L1), MOS general-purpose logic (L2a), MOS gate arrays (L2b), MOS standard cells and field-programmable logic (L2c), MOS display drivers (L3), MOS touch-screen controllers (L4) and MOS special-purpose logic (LA).
evidence_found: "This category contains the following subcategories; Digital Bipolar (code L1) MOS General Purpose Logic (code L2a) MOS Gate Arrays (code L2b) MOS Standard Cells and Field Programmable Logic (code L2c) MOS Display Drivers (code L3) MOS Touch Screen Controller (code L4) MOS Special Purpose Logic (code LA)" (s.3.4.3, p.17); "L99 Total Logic. Total of items L1, L2a to L2c, L3, L4 and LA (L5 to L9)." (p.21)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). This is the 2021 edition. Later editions are behind a subscriber login.

original_interpretation: WSTS MOS special-purpose logic (LA) holds application-specific standard products (ASSPs) designed by the chip maker and customer-specific ICs (CSICs) designed by the customer, each designed for one application segment.
evidence_found: "LA. MOS Special Purpose Logic – The devices in this category are either (i) Application Specific Standard Products (ASSP) designed by semiconductor manufacturer or (ii) Customer Specific Integrated Circuits (CSIC) designed by the customer, all of which are specifically designed for one of the application segments listed below." (p.19)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). Touch-screen controllers are excluded and go to L4. On p.20 the manufacturer 'assumes circuit design responsibility' for CSICs initiated by a customer's specification.

original_interpretation: WSTS splits MOS special-purpose logic into five application segments: consumer (L5), computer and peripherals (L6), communication (L7), automotive (L8) and multipurpose and other (L9).
evidence_found: "MOS Special Purpose Logic (code LA) contains the following subcategories, i.e. Consumer (code L5), Computer and Peripherals (code L6), Communication (code L7), Automotive (code L8) and Multipurpose and Other (code L9)." (p.20)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004).

original_interpretation: WSTS defines an ASSP as a chip whose design is controlled by the semiconductor maker to fill an application-specific need, listed in catalogues and sold to any customer.
evidence_found: "Application Specific Standard Products (ASSP) are designed or their design is controlled by the semiconductor manufacturer to fill an application specific need in a given market segment. The manufacturer lists the devices in catalogs and sells them to any customer." (p.19)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004).

original_interpretation: WSTS counts a customer-specific IC (CSIC, 'full custom') under special-purpose logic only when its application is evident and sizeable; all other CSICs go to MOS gate arrays (L2b) or MOS standard cells (L2c).
evidence_found: "These ICs are sometimes called \"Full Custom\". This category should only include those CSICs for which the application is obviously evident to semiconductor manufacturer and for which the application market is relatively sizable, such as ICs for watches. All other CSICs shall be classified in MOS Gate Arrays (code L2b) or MOS Standard Cells (code L2c)." (p.20)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004).

original_interpretation: WSTS reports FPGAs, PLDs and PALs (field-programmable logic devices) in category L2c together with standard-cell CSICs, split by application.
evidence_found: Under "L2c. MOS Standard Cells and Field Programmable Logic": "Some typical examples are Programmable Logic Devices (PLD), Programmable Array Logics (PAL) and Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGA)." ... "these devices shall be reported into the subcategories listed below according to the application" (L2e-L2j) (pp.18-19)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). Only FPL devices sold as standard parts for field programming count here. FPL-based catalogue ASICs from the chip maker go to Micro or other logic categories.

original_interpretation: WSTS MOS general-purpose logic (L2a) is standard commodity catalogue logic such as simple gates, flip-flops and registers, excluding programmable devices and ASICs.
evidence_found: "L2a. MOS General Purpose Logic - Devices in this classification are standard commodity catalog products, usually simple gates, flip-flop circuits and registers. ... Excluded are catalog products of any programmable device or any Special Purpose Application Specific (ASIC) device." (p.17)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004).

original_interpretation: WSTS classifies smartphone and tablet application processors (integrating CPU, GPU, connectivity and codecs, with or without modem) as logic (L7f, wireless communication under special-purpose logic), not as micro ICs.
evidence_found: "L7f. Wireless Communication – Application Processor. ICs designed for low power applications, especially smartphones, tablets, portable media players, etc., which integrate multiple components including central processing unit, graphic processing unit and connectivity, as well as multimedia codec. Application Processors which also integrate a modem should be reported in this category L7f, too." (p.21)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). L7f sits under L7 Communication within LA (hierarchy table, p.3). The 'not micro' part follows from the multi-core rule on p.13.

original_interpretation: Under WSTS rules, a maker-designed IC with multiple functional cores including an MPU, MCU or DSP core is reported as logic, not micro; only 'pure' or core-dominant MPU/MCU/DSP products are micro.
evidence_found: "MOS Micro shall include (i) \"pure\" MPU, MCU and DSP products and (ii) MPU-, MCU-, or DSP-dominant products" ... "ICs, designed by semiconductor manufacturer and having multiple functional cores including MPU-, MCU- or DSP-core, are NOT to be reported in this MOS Micro category, but to be reported under appropriate MOS Logic categories (code L)" (s.3.4.2, p.13)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004).

original_interpretation: WSTS 'Total Application Specific ICs' (Q99) is not reported by members but computed by data-collection agents as the sum of application-specific analog, MCUs, DSPs, standard cells/FPLDs and special-purpose logic.
evidence_found: "Q99 Total Application Specific ICs – Total of items JA (JB to JF), P2 (P51, P52 and P6), P4, L2c (L2e to L2j), and LA (L5 to L9)" ... "Items in Q99 (i.e. Q1 to Q6) are NOT to be reported by member companies. They are mathematical aggregation of world totals ... Mathematical aggregation is performed by Data Collecting Agencies (DCAs)." (s.3.4.5, pp.24-25)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). P2 covers all MCUs, including general-purpose MCUs (P51), so Q99 is broader than 'application-specific' suggests.

original_interpretation: WSTS splits analog ICs into general-purpose analog (J0: amplifiers/comparators, signal conversion, interface, power management) and application-specific analog (JA: consumer, computer, communications, automotive, industrial and others).
evidence_found: "This Analog category contains General Purpose Analog (code J0) and Application Specific Analog (code JA) subcategories. The General Purpose Analog category is sub-divided into specific functional subcategories of Amplifiers/Comparators (Signal Conditioning), Signal Conversion, Interface, and Power Management ICs." (p.8); JB Consumer, JC Computer, JD Communications, JE Automotive, JF Industrial & Others (pp.10-12)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). The quote is on p.8, not p.7 as the researcher recorded.

original_interpretation: WSTS assigns mixed-signal chips to digital or analog by chip area: an IC is analog if at least 50% of its die area is analog circuitry.
evidence_found: "J. Analog. Devices are classified as ANALOG if at least 50% of the total die area of the integrated circuit(s) in the device is occupied by ANALOG circuitry." (s.3.4.1, p.7); s.3.4: "Circuits combining digital and analog techniques are classified into digital circuits or analog circuits according to the chip area devoted to the respective technique."
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). Caveats in the source: s.3.4 says analog needs 'greater than 50 percent', not 'at least'. A device whose area is close to 50% may also be deemed analog if its essential function is analog signal processing.

original_interpretation: WSTS counts image sensors (CCD and CMOS image sensors) and all optical sensors in optoelectronics, not in sensors and actuators.
evidence_found: "F5. Image Sensors ... F5a. CCD & Other Image Sensors ... F5b. CMOS Image Sensors" (s.3.2, p.7); "NOTE: All optical sensors are to be reported in the appropriate category of Optoelectronics." (s.3.3, p.7)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). Light sensors (F10) and infrared (F7) are also in optoelectronics.

original_interpretation: The WSTS 2021 classification includes solar cells in optoelectronics, under 'Other Optoelectronics' (F6).
evidence_found: "F6. Other Optoelectronics - All other optoelectronics devices not specifically listed above, including fiber optic components and solar cells." (s.3.2, p.7)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). This corrects the earlier 'no match for solar' result behind CLM-0016.

original_interpretation: WSTS sensors and actuators (H99) cover temperature and other non-optical sensors, pressure sensors, acceleration and yaw-rate sensors, magnetic-field sensors, and actuators such as ink-jet nozzles, micro-mirrors, solid-state relays and SAW filters.
evidence_found: "H1 Temperature & Other Sensors - All devices for measurement of temperature ... and all other non-optical sensors"; "H2 Pressure Sensors"; "H3 Acceleration and Yaw Rate Sensors"; "H4 Magnetic Field Sensors"; "H6. Actuators ... This includes, but is not limited to, ink jet nozzles, micro mirrors, solid-state relays, and SAW filters." (s.3.3, p.7)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004).

original_interpretation: WSTS counts IGBTs, IGBT modules and MOSFET power transistors (power dissipation of 1W or more) as discrete power transistors, with separate value and unit reporting for bipolar/other, IGBT and MOSFET power-transistor groups.
evidence_found: "C. Power Transistors. Transistors with a power dissipation of 1W or more ... insulated gate bipolar transistors (IGBT)" (p.4-5); "all Power Transistors under this category C shall be classified into the following three products groups, and total dollar value sold in each region and Total Worldwide, and the Total Worldwide Units shall be reported ... CA. Bipolar and Other ... CB. Insulated Gate Bipolar Transistors ... CC. MOSFET Power Transistors" (p.5)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). IGBTs and FETs below 1W are small-signal transistors (B2), not power transistors.

original_interpretation: The WSTS 2021 classification has no separate product category for silicon-carbide or gallium-nitride devices: product classes are defined by function (e.g. power transistor, rectifier), and silicon carbide appears only as an example semiconductor material.
evidence_found: Full-text search of the extracted text for 'silicon carbide', 'SiC', 'GaN', 'gallium': the only hit is s.2.1 (p.3): "Examples: Germanium, silicon, III V compounds such as gallium arsenide or polycrystalline materials such as selenium, silicon carbide, cadmium sulfide, zinc oxide, organic compounds." Power categories C1-C11 are defined by device type, power rating and voltage.
notes: Interpretation confirmed by my own search. Scope is limited to the 2021 edition. s.2.1 also says products 'may be fabricated ... from any material', which supports the material-neutral reading. Later editions (2023+) are behind the SIA subscriber login and were not checked.

original_interpretation: The 2021 WSTS classification has no explicit categories for HBM, data-center GPUs or AI accelerators: 'graphic processing unit' appears only inside the smartphone application-processor definition, and memory is split only into DRAM, SRAM, mask ROM/EPROM, flash and other memory.
evidence_found: My own search: no match for 'HBM', 'stack', 'GPU', 'accelerat' (except acceleration sensors); 'graphic processing unit' occurs only in L7f (p.21). "MOS Memory contains the following subcategories; DRAM (M1) SRAM (M2) Mask Programmable ROM & EPROM (M8) Flash Memory (M7) Other Memory (M6)" (s.3.4.4, p.22)
notes: Interpretation confirmed. 'Split only into' refers to the top-level memory split. Below it, DRAM is split by density and flash by NOR/NAND and density. This is the 2021 edition only.

original_interpretation: WSTS counts memory units at device level: a memory module is counted as its number of component chips, and partially good memories are prorated by the share of functional bits.
evidence_found: "A company makes a DRAM module containing nine 128M DRAM devices. The company sells 50,000 modules in a month, and ... reports 450,000 units in the TOTAL WORLDWIDE UNIT column." and "if 1000 units of products are shipped that have 50% of bits functional, the quantity reported to WSTS should be 500 units." (s.3.4.4, p.22)
notes: Checked against the text layer of the PDF (pypdf extraction of SRC-0004). Revenue for partially good parts is reported at actual value. DRAM and NAND units are also translated into bit-equivalent totals (M1x, M7Bx-z).

original_interpretation: The WSTS End Use Report for a year is built from that year's annual Blue Book market totals, using the higher-level product classification.
evidence_found: "End Use Report 2020, to be issued around the end of February 2021, is generated based on the annual total 2020 market data compiled in the Blue Book reports for 2020. Thus, End Use Report 2020 will be based on (i) higher level of product classifications for 2020" (s.1(b), p.2); the 2018 edition says the same for End Use Report 2017.
notes: The 2021 text states this for 2020 specifically. Generalising to 'a year' is supported because the 2018 edition uses identical wording for 2017. Both editions also tie the report to that year's region definitions.

original_interpretation: In 2024 MPUs were US$54.2 billion (+19.6%), MCUs US$21.8 billion (-21.9%) and DSPs US$2.7 billion (-15.6%) of worldwide sales (SIA Factbook).
evidence_found: 2025 SIA Factbook, p. 9 chart 'Annual Semiconductor Shipments by product type ($ Billion)'; the PDF text layer lists values $2.7, $18.9, $21.8, $31.0, $41.1, $54.2, $79.6, $165.5, $215.8 against labels DSP, Sensor, MCU, Discretes, Opto, MPU, Analog, Memory, Logic, and growths +20.8% ... +19.6% ... -21.9% ... -15.6%. "Source: World Semiconductor Trade Statistics (WSTS) and SIA Estimates."
notes: Value-to-label mapping checked against the text layer and the page image. Cross-check: MPU+MCU+DSP = $78.7bn, which matches the WSTS 2024 Micro total of US$78,633M (SRC-0002). Labelled WSTS data plus SIA estimates, so it is not purely a WSTS actual.

original_interpretation: SIA states that logic, memory, analog and MPU accounted for almost 80% of 2024 semiconductor sales; their chart values (US$515.1bn of US$630.6bn) imply about 82%.
evidence_found: "In recent years, the largest segments of the worldwide semiconductor industry have been logic, memory, analog, and MPU. In 2024, these products accounted for almost 80 percent of semiconductor industry sales." (2025 Factbook, p. 9); chart: Logic $215.8, Memory $165.5, Analog $79.6, MPU $54.2; all nine bars sum to $630.6
notes: My own arithmetic: 515.1/630.6 = 81.7%. SIA's 'almost 80 percent' understates its own chart. The metric value of 80 records SIA's statement.

original_interpretation: In 2024 communications was 33.0% of global semiconductor demand, second to computers/AI at 34.9% (WSTS End Use Survey via SIA).
evidence_found: SIA SOI 2025, p. 24, 'TOTAL GLOBAL DEMAND SHARE BY END USE, 2024'. The text layer gives a two-column grid: left Computers/AI 34.9%, Communications 33.0%, Automotive 12.7%; right Consumer Electronics 9.9%, Industrial Applications 8.4%, Government 1.0%. "Source: WSTS, 2024 End Use Survey". The Factbook 2025 p. 8 pie and the SOI 2026 p. 8 (2024: 35%/33%) agree.
notes: I checked the label mapping independently from the text-layer order and the page images of all three SIA documents. Newer data: in 2025 communications fell to 28.7% (SOI 2026, already in CLM-1346).

original_interpretation: In 2024 automotive was 12.7% of global semiconductor demand, consumer 9.9%, industrial 8.4% and government 1.0% (WSTS End Use Survey via SIA).
evidence_found: SIA SOI 2025 p. 24 chart grid: "Automotive" 12.7% (left column, third row), "Consumer Electronics" 9.9%, "Industrial Applications" 8.4%, "Government" 1.0% (right column); Factbook 2025 p. 8 pie, same values; SOI 2026 p. 8 bars for 2024: Automotive 13%, Consumer Electronics 10%, Industrial 8%, Government 1%
notes: All three SIA documents agree. This supports CON-0041 favouring CLM-1343 over CLM-0561 (automotive 9.9%). Values are rounded chart labels, not a data table.

original_interpretation: SIA reports that from 2023 to 2024 the computer segment's share of chip sales rose 10 points to become the largest; communications, consumer and government sales rose while auto and industrial declined.
evidence_found: "Most notably, the computer market's share of chip sales increased by 10% from 2023 to become the largest segment in 2024. Other segments showed varied sales performance: communications, consumer electronics, and government sectors saw increases, while auto and industrial sales declined." (SIA SOI 2025, p. 24)
notes: SIA writes '10%', not '10 points'. The points reading is right: the 2024 Factbook gives PC/computer at 25% in 2023, and 34.9% in 2024 is +9.9 pp. Implied dollar sales check out: auto 17%x$526.9bn = $89.6bn falls to 12.7%x$630.5bn = $80.1bn; consumer rises from $58.0bn to $62.4bn.

original_interpretation: Sales of automotive ICs grew 23.7% to a record US$42.2 billion in 2023 (SIA, WSTS data).
evidence_found: "And sales of automotive ICs grew by 23.7% year-over-year to a record total of $42.2 billion." (SIA press release, 5 Feb 2024)
notes: Consistent with the 2022 base of $34.1bn (SRC-0108): 42.2/34.1 = +23.8%. SIA does not define 'automotive ICs' in the release; reading it as WSTS application-specific automotive ICs is plausible but not stated.

original_interpretation: Sales of automotive ICs grew 29.2% to a record US$34.1 billion in 2022 (SIA, WSTS data).
evidence_found: "Sales of automotive ICs grew by 29.2% year-over-year to a record total of $34.1 billion." (SIA press release, 3 Feb 2023; "This release reflects updated sales data released on March 3, 2023")
notes: Consistent with the 2021 base of $26.4bn: 34.1/26.4 = +29.2%. The release was updated with March 2023 data. The page title says 3.3%; the URL slug says 3-2.

original_interpretation: Sales of automotive ICs were a record US$26.4 billion in 2021, up 34.3% (SIA, WSTS data).
evidence_found: "Sales of automotive ICs increased 34.3% year-over-year to a record high of $26.4 billion." (SIA press release, 14 Feb 2022)

original_interpretation: SIA reported that the industry shipped a record 1.15 trillion semiconductor units in 2021, worth US$555.9 billion.
evidence_found: "Industry sold 1.15 trillion semiconductors totaling $555.9 billion in 2021, both records" (SIA press release, 14 Feb 2022, subtitle)
notes: The $555.9bn 2021 total is unchanged in SIA's Feb 2023 release (SRC-0108: 'compared to the 2021 total of $555.9 billion').

original_interpretation: SIA's 2026 report groups AI-server chips as 'advanced logic' (AI accelerators, ASICs, FPGAs, CPUs, DPUs, networking chips), memory (HBM, DRAM, SRAM, NAND) and 'analog/foundational' chips (power chips, transceivers, controllers, sensors).
evidence_found: "• Advanced logic chips, such as AI accelerators, application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), central processing units (CPUs), data processing units (DPUs), and networking chips; • Memory, such as high-bandwidth memory (HBM), dynamic and static random-access memory (DRAM and SRAM), and non-volatile flash memory (NAND); and • Analog/foundational chips, such as power chips, transceivers, controllers, and sensors" (SIA SOI 2026, p. 9)
notes: SIA attributes this grouping to 'a recent SIA-Deloitte report'. It is a descriptive taxonomy, not the WSTS classification.

original_interpretation: SIA reports that 'foundational chip' sales in 2025 were still 5.2% below their 2022 peak.
evidence_found: "Foundational chip sales remain constrained, with sales down 5.2% in 2025 compared to their highest revenue total in 2022." (SIA SOI 2026, p. 6)
notes: SIA does not define 'foundational chips' on p. 6, so the population is unclear.

original_interpretation: SIA reports that foundational chip sales volume rose 6.3% in 2025 versus 2024, while their value stayed below the 2022 peak, meaning unit prices fell.
evidence_found: "Foundational chip sales remain constrained, with sales down 5.2% in 2025 compared to their highest revenue total in 2022. Foundational chip sales volume, however, increased modestly at 6.3% in 2025 compared to 2024." (SIA SOI 2026, p. 6)
correction: SIA supports only the +6.3% volume growth for 2025 vs 2024. 'Meaning unit prices fell' does not follow: value is compared with 2022 and volume with 2024. A superseding claim drops the inference.
notes: SIA gives no 2025-vs-2024 value change for foundational chips. As a rough proxy, WSTS non-logic, non-memory sales grew from US$249.3bn (2024) to US$266.1bn (2025), about +6.7% (SRC-0002/SRC-0001), roughly in line with +6.3% volume. That points to flat average prices, not falling ones, but SIA's category may differ. The claim is typed 'fact' but bundles an inference.

original_interpretation: SIA states that overcapacity in foundational chips in China is distorting the market and depressing prices.
evidence_found: "Similarly, foundational chip overcapacity in China is distorting the market and depressing prices." (SIA SOI 2026, p. 20)
notes: This is SIA's advocacy view, correctly typed reported_claim. The report gives no data for it.
